paras: The attacks on Black sailors at Bar Harbor were a series of assaults in July 1903 in which white enlisted men from a fleet of United States warships drove Black crewmen out of a naval YMCA tent and beat and chased them through the streets of Bar Harbor, Maine.
No one was reported killed, and after the night of the attacks Black sailors were reported to stay off the shore after dark.
Northern papers reported the clash as a "race war" in the navy, and Southern editorials later used it to argue against the enlistment of Black men.

A fleet of seven United States warships lay in the harbor at Bar Harbor in July 1903. According to the Washington Times, the seven crews included seven Black men, whose white shipmates had "shown the same race prejudice which other sailors feel." A Bar Harbor dispatch to the New-York Tribune said the white sailors had been "making it unpleasant" for the Black crewmen since the fleet arrived, so that the latter had mostly stayed aboard rather than risk abuse in the streets.

On a Saturday night some of the Black sailors came ashore, and the Washington Times reported "numerous fights" in the streets between white and Black sailors. About midnight several white "jackies" entered the tent that the naval branch of the Young Men's Christian Association had put up in the town park and drove out the Black sailors who had gone there to lodge for the night.

Two Black sailors were knocked down on Main Street by a crowd of sailors and, after "a few kicks and punches," got up and ran. One was thrown over a board fence into the street; the Washington Times said he was thrown "over a board fence and back again." Another reached the police station, where he was locked up to keep him from the sailors chasing him, and a third ran into a drug store, was hidden in the cellar and later left by a back door across the yards. The New York Sun's correspondent wrote that both men "begged for protection" from the white sailors pursuing them.

Afterward no Black sailors came ashore after dark, and the Sun reported that their shore leave would be stopped to avoid further clashes. No victims or attackers were named, and the coverage shows no arrests, naval inquiry or punishment.

The story broke on July 21 in the New-York Tribune, which ran it under the headline "Race War on Warships" with the subhead "Negroes in the Crews Tormented by the White Sailors" and listed it in its front-page news summary. The same day the Washington Times headed its version "Uncle Sam's Jackies Don't Like Negroes," and the Minneapolis Journal printed the New York Sun's shorter account as "Jackies' Race War." Over the next week the text ran as "Color Line in the Navy" in the Rock Island Argus, as "Race War in the Navy" in the Annapolis Evening Capital, subheaded "Monkey And Parrot Time," and in South Carolina weeklies.

Southern commentary turned the incident against the Roosevelt administration's policy toward Black Americans. The Manning Times repeated The State's remark that the Black sailors were "so beaten and abused" ashore that they stayed aboard, and asked what the commander-in-chief would do. A Baltimore Sun editorial reprinted in Birmingham predicted that white men would refuse to enlist alongside Black sailors, and the St. Landry Clarion, under the headline "The Navy and the Coon," cited "the beating of negro sailors at Bar Harbor by their white shipmates" as evidence that Black men should be removed from the navy.
All of the coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report of the Bar Harbor attacks was found.

The accounts differ on the date: the Tribune's dispatch of July 20 placed the attacks on "last Saturday night," July 18, while the Sun's dispatch, dated July 21 in the Minneapolis Journal, placed the tent expulsion "about midnight last night." On severity, the first reports describe "a few kicks and punches," while a Baltimore Sun editorial weeks later said the white sailors "beat many of them severely."

bases: Crowds of white sailors drove Black crewmen from a lodging tent, knocked down, kicked and chased them through the streets (A2, A3, A4); no killing and no wider community was targeted.

accounts.label: Bar Harbor dispatch of July 20 (Tribune / New York Times text)
accounts.gist: White sailors had harassed the Black crewmen since the fleet arrived; on Saturday night about midnight they drove Black men from the YMCA tent, knocked down two on Main Street, threw one over a fence and chased others into the police station and a drug store.

accounts.label: Washington Times dispatch of July 21
accounts.gist: Seven Black men in seven crews; Saturday night brought 'numerous fights' between white and Black sailors, the tent expulsion and two knockdowns.

accounts.label: New York Sun special
accounts.gist: Whites rushed Black sailors from the YMCA tent 'about midnight last night'; two fled to the police station and a drug store begging protection; shore leave to be withheld from Black sailors.

accounts.label: Southern editorials
accounts.gist: White sailors beat 'many' Black sailors 'severely'; the episode shows that race friction in the navy will force the government to exclude Black men or face white refusal to enlist.

framing.detail: New-York Tribune: 'Race War on Warships. Negroes in the Crews Tormented by the White Sailors'; places blame on the white sailors' 'race feeling'.
Washington Times: 'Uncle Sam's Jackies Don't Like Negroes'; treats white sailors' 'race prejudice' as common to sailors.
Minneapolis Journal, Rock Island Argus and South Carolina weeklies ran the Sun or Tribune/Times text as 'Jackies' Race War', 'Color Line in the Navy', 'Race War in Navy'.
Annapolis Evening Capital headed the dispatch 'Black And White Jackies Ashore At Bar Harbor Have Monkey And Parrot Time', treating the attacks as farce.
Manning Times, quoting The State, used the beatings to needle the President rather than condemn the attackers.
Baltimore Sun (via Age-Herald) and St. Landry Clarion ('The Navy and the Coon') treated the beating as proof that Black men must be kept out of the navy.
